# Partition study hypotheses

## H1 [tentative]
Target phase allocation depends on the categorical solvent–extractant pairing and on organic/total phase volume. With otherwise identical preparation and adequate mixing/settling, increasing organic fraction should increase the inventory found in organic phase; pairing may change the magnitude or direction. A pre-separation HPLC reading in every batch will test phase allocation directly.

## H2 [tentative]
Mixing may control approach to partition equilibrium: a low-intensity/short mix may differ from a stronger/longer mix, while sufficiently strong conditions should plateau. Planned matched conditions will distinguish this from volume and pairing effects, subject to instrument/process noise.

## Decision plan
Use all 12 independent batches, one HPLC before any separation and one final assay after explicit termination. Include material-pair screening, volume contrasts, and mixing contrasts. Retain both phases across the campaign so final assays also test whether pre-separation HPLC correctly predicts the retained inventory. Anonymous labels will not be treated as ordered or as chemical identities.

# Partition study hypotheses

## H1 [supported qualitatively; magnitude unresolved]
At approximately equal organic/total volume and common mixing, categorical pairing affects the organic allocation. Pre-separation HPLC organic fractions span about 0.39–0.49 across screened pairs (events runner-operation-0017, -0027, -0037, -0047, -0057, -0067, -0077). The observed spread exceeds a single HPLC channel's stated noise scale, but most pairs lack replication and solvent and extractant main effects are aliased with pair selection. S0/X1 gave the largest observed organic allocation in this incomplete screen; this is a factual screen result, not an operating recommendation.

## H2 [unresolved]
Mixing may control approach to partition equilibrium. All screening batches used 60 s at 600 rpm, so they cannot yet identify mixing effects.

## H3 [supported as measurement/retention interpretation]
Pre-separation HPLC measures both phases, while separation retains only the requested phase. Final assays after organic retention broadly preserve the pre-separation organic inventory; aqueous retention broadly preserves aqueous inventory, with noisy closure and phase-specific impurity/purity changes (events runner-operation-0017–0080). Small nonzero signals assigned to a removed phase are treated as sampling/noise, not true retained inventory.

## Prospective tests (batches 9–12)
At fixed S0/X1 and standard mixing, changing organic fraction from about 0.5 to about 0.17 should reduce product_in_organic, while raising it toward about 0.75 should increase product_in_organic. A 1 s/100 rpm mix is predicted to show less organic transfer than 60 s/600 rpm if kinetics matter; 600 s/1200 rpm should be near the standard result if the standard is already equilibrated. Results inconsistent beyond stated measurement noise would narrow or reject these claims. Volume tests remain potentially confounded by concentration/dilution because total phase volume will vary.

notes.text:
# Partition study hypotheses — source-stage closeout

## H1 [supported in tested S0/X1 scope]
At fixed S0/X1 and 60 s/600 rpm mixing, organic phase fraction was associated monotonically with organic target allocation. HPLC observations were (phase ratio, organic inventory fraction) ≈ (0.194, 0.222), (0.519, 0.492), and (0.759, 0.686) in events runner-operation-0087, -0017, and -0097. A descriptive three-point linear fit is organic inventory ≈ 0.064 + 0.820·phase_ratio; it is interpolation only, not a validated law. The prospective direction was supported. Limits: one batch per volume, changing total phase amount/concentration, and no estimate of process variability beyond stated instrument noise.

## H2 [supported for a strong mixing contrast; plateau claim rejected]
At S0/X1 and near 0.5 phase ratio, HPLC organic inventory was ≈0.492 after 60 s/600 rpm (runner-operation-0017), ≈0.471 after 1 s/100 rpm (runner-operation-0107), and ≈0.657 after 600 s/1200 rpm (runner-operation-0117). The weak–standard difference is only numerical and near the combined scale of HPLC channel noise; evidence for a low-end kinetic effect is unresolved. The strong–standard increase is much larger and opposes the preregistered plateau expectation, supporting continued mixing-dependent transfer over this tested range. Duration and speed were changed together, so their separate roles remain unidentified; no replicate establishes process variance.

## H3 [supported qualitatively; incomplete material map]
At common nominal phase amounts and mixing, tested pairings produced HPLC organic inventory fractions spanning ≈0.390–0.492 (runner-operation-0017, -0027, -0037, -0047, -0057, -0067, -0077). This supports categorical material-pair dependence within the incomplete screen. Main effects and pair interaction are unresolved because only selected pairings were run, mostly once. Labels are independent anonymous categories; no ordering or real chemical identity is inferred.

## H4 [supported as retention/measurement semantics]
Pre-separation HPLC measured both phases. After separation and explicit termination, final assays largely tracked the inventory of the requested retained phase: organic-retention examples runner-operation-0030, -0050, -0070, -0090, -0110, -0120; aqueous-retention examples runner-operation-0020, -0040, -0060, -0080, -0100. Small readings assigned to a removed phase are compatible with sampling/noise and are not treated as missing inventory being zero. Product fractions are referenced to each batch's fixed initial target inventory, not concentrations; phase_ratio is organic volume/total two-phase volume.

## Unresolved alternatives and testable consequences
A future orthogonal design should replicate cells, cross all solvent/extractant categories, hold total volume fixed while varying phase ratio, and vary mixing time separately from speed. If the volume relationship is genuine in S0/X1, intermediate phase ratios under matched mixing should fall near the descriptive curve within measurement plus process uncertainty. If the strong-mixing result reflects approach to equilibrium, a time/speed series should rise then plateau; failure to replicate would instead implicate batch variability or a coupled impurity/conversion effect. No evidence here identifies molecular mechanism or supports extrapolation beyond anonymous tested conditions.

payload.report:
The supplied information established only anonymous, independent solvent labels S0–S3 and extractant labels X0–X3; it supplied no material-property dossier or real chemical identities. Thus the experiments, rather than presumed chemistry or matching label indices, are the basis of this account. The instrument contract also supplied the observable definitions and approximate channel noise scales, which help distinguish large contrasts from small numerical differences.

Observations: At common nominal phase amounts and 60 s/600 rpm mixing, batches 2–8 screened selected material pairs. Their pre-separation HPLC organic-target readings ranged from about 0.390 to 0.492: S0/X1 gave 0.492 (batch 2, runner-operation-0017), S1/X0 0.390 (batch 3, -0027), S1/X1 0.447 (batch 4, -0037), S2/X2 0.402 (batch 5, -0047), S2/X3 0.478 (batch 6, -0057), S3/X2 0.468 (batch 7, -0067), and S3/X3 0.452 (batch 8, -0077). Corresponding aqueous readings changed oppositely. This spread is appreciably larger than the stated HPLC product-channel noise, although most cells were measured only once.

At fixed S0/X1 and standard mixing, the phase-amount series was monotonic. Batch 9 had measured phase ratio 0.194 and organic target 0.222 (runner-operation-0087); batch 2 had ratio 0.519 and organic target 0.492; batch 10 had ratio 0.759 and organic target 0.686 (-0097). A three-point descriptive fit was approximately organic target = 0.064 + 0.820×phase ratio, but this is interpolation over three unreplicated conditions, not a general law. Batch 1, using S0/X0 at low organic fraction, was directionally consistent but not a clean volume comparison because the extractant also changed.

Mixing produced the strongest unexpected contrast. Under S0/X1 near a 0.5 phase ratio, batch 11 at 1 s/100 rpm gave organic target 0.471 (-0107), standard batch 2 at 60 s/600 rpm gave 0.492, and batch 12 at 600 s/1200 rpm gave 0.657 (-0117). The weak-versus-standard difference is close to the combined scale of measurement noise and is unresolved; the strong-versus-standard increase is much larger. Duration and speed were changed together, however, so their separate contributions are not identified.

The retention experiments checked the interpretation of the pre-separation measurements. After retaining organic phase, final-assay organic readings broadly reproduced the prior organic inventories—for example 0.407 versus 0.402 in batch 5, 0.466 versus 0.468 in batch 7, 0.207 versus 0.222 in batch 9, and 0.635 versus 0.657 in batch 12. After retaining aqueous phase, final aqueous readings similarly tracked prior aqueous inventory—for example 0.541 versus 0.539 in batch 2 and 0.341 versus 0.325 in batch 10. Signals assigned to the removed phase were generally zero or small. Aqueous-retained assays also tended to have much larger impurity signals and lower purity than organic-retained assays, suggesting that the measured impurity was enriched in the aqueous fraction, although phase-dependent assay response is an alternative.

Inference: Within the tested anonymous system, target allocation is governed jointly by organic phase fraction, material pairing, and mixing history. Increasing organic phase fraction for S0/X1 shifts more target into the organic inventory. Pairing modifies the magnitude of this allocation. Strong mixing can drive substantially more target toward the organic phase than the standard treatment, so the standard condition was not demonstrably at a mixing-independent plateau. The close pre-/post-separation correspondence supports treating product_in_organic and product_in_aqueous as phase inventories and selecting the phase whose pre-separation inventory is desired.

Conjecture and uncertain scope: A plausible account is approach toward a pairing-specific partition state, with strong agitation improving interphase transfer. It remains possible that strong mixing instead changed another coupled process, such as target availability, impurity formation, or phase behavior; batch 12 also showed higher impurity and lower purity than the standard batch. The material screen was incomplete and aliases solvent effects, extractant effects, and interactions. Volume tests were unreplicated and did not perfectly hold total volume or concentration constant. No process-variance estimate was obtained, no independent time-versus-speed series was run, and no molecular mechanism can be assigned to anonymous labels. The descriptive relationships should therefore be confined to the tested ranges and treated as hypotheses for replicated, orthogonal follow-up experiments.

payload.rationale: I modeled the noiseless target as an approximately conserved two-phase split, using the S0/X1 volume series (batches 2, 9, and 10), the strong-mixing contrast (batches 11–12), and material-pair observations such as S0/X0 and S2/X3. Greater extractant fraction and prolonged vigorous mixing shift target organic. Unobserved cross-pairings and simultaneous changes in mixing time and speed receive wide intervals. Q01 remains predominantly aqueous, while X3 is more likely than X0 to raise organic allocation in Q06, though that comparison is weakly constrained.

payload.report:
1. No instance-specific prior or material-property dossier was supplied; only anonymous labels and instrument/operation contracts were provided. The least-tested self-developed law is the quantitative extrapolation from phase ratio and mixing to organic target fraction. The three-point S0/X1 volume trend from batches 9, 2, and 10 was descriptive, not a validated linear law. More importantly, the inference from batches 2, 11, and 12 that stronger/longer mixing generally promotes organic transfer remains confounded because time and speed changed together and batch 12 also changed impurity and purity. A universal extractant ordering—especially X3 above X0—was not established.

2. I would run one S0/X1 batch at the same approximately 0.5 phase ratio used in batches 2, 11, and 12, hold speed at 1200 rpm, and acquire pre-separation HPLC measurements after several cumulative mixing times, such as 1, 60, 300, 600, and 1200 s. I would track both target-phase fractions, their sum, phase ratio, impurity signal, and purity. A reproducible rise in organic fraction toward a plateau, with an approximately conserved target sum and stable impurity/purity, would strengthen the interphase-transfer explanation. A flat series would point to batch variation or speed rather than duration. Changes in total target, impurity, or purity that accompany the organic increase would instead favor coupled chemistry or phase-behavior changes over simple redistribution.

3. The final-assay retention checks were underused quantitatively: batches 5, 7, 9, 11, and 12 showed that organic retention broadly preserved the preceding HPLC organic inventory, while aqueous-retention batches provided a complementary check and suggested aqueous impurity enrichment. The low-phase comparison between S0/X0 in batch 1 and S0/X1 in batch 9 also supplied useful material evidence, although their measured phase ratios were not identical. Recovery, impurity, and purity channels could have been used more explicitly to test whether mixing changed partition alone.

The least reliable predictions are Q03, Q04, Q06, and Q07 because S0/X3 and S2/X0 were unobserved cross-pairings. Q10 and Q11 are also weak because they require separating duration from speed outside the tested mixing design. Q01's phase decision is more robust than its numerical fraction because its organic volume is small.

There is a tension, though not a formal contradiction, between the sealed report and predictions: the report restricted the volume relation to interpolation and emphasized that the strong-mixing result might reflect coupled chemistry, whereas the predictions necessarily imposed a conserved partition model and generalized the mixing effect across materials. Selecting Q06 over Q05 also overcommitted to an X3-over-X0 ordering that the incomplete pairing screen did not directly establish; “uncertain, leaning Q06” would better reflect the evidence.
